questions.set_intro: Imagine that a weekend magazine wants a story about your city. You agreed to answer a few questions by phone about how people spend Saturday.
questions.question: What do you usually do on Saturday morning?
questions.model_answer: On Saturday morning I tidy my room, eat a late breakfast, and then walk to the market. I try not to schedule any appointments before noon.

questions.set_intro: Imagine that a weekend magazine wants a story about your city. You agreed to answer a few questions by phone about how people spend Saturday.
questions.question: Do you prefer a busy Saturday or a quiet one? Why?
questions.model_answer: I prefer a quiet Saturday to a packed one. The workweek is already full of messages, so an empty morning helps me feel ready again.

questions.set_intro: Imagine that a weekend magazine wants a story about your city. You agreed to answer a few questions by phone about how people spend Saturday.
questions.question: A friend says the weekend should be used only for rest. Do you agree? Why or why not?
questions.model_answer: I partly agree, but I would not use the whole weekend only for rest. One quiet morning is important, and I protect mine. The rest of Saturday can still hold friends, errands, or a class, because those activities belong in a good week too. Rest works best as a real break, not as two empty days that push every chore to Sunday night.

questions.question: When a manager gives feedback, is it better to do it in writing or face to face? Choose one and give reasons for your opinion.
questions.model_answer: I think a manager should give feedback face to face rather than only in writing. Tone is easy to misread in a message, and a short note can sound colder than the manager intended, especially when the comment is about a mistake. In person, the employee can ask a question immediately, and the manager can show a better example. I would still follow the talk with a few brief written points, so both people remember what was agreed. The written record is useful, but it should support the conversation rather than replace it. A face-to-face talk is clearer and less likely to leave someone worrying for the rest of the day. Talking first and writing second keeps the feedback both kind and specific.
